name: Yara Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll just say what I think, I'm not going to make speeches.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick at a pharmacy supplies warehouse on the industrial estate behind the hospital. It's small boxes, tablets, creams, plasters, going into grey totes for chemist shops, and you have to be careful because a wrong pick is a wrong medicine. Eight till four, a handheld scanner, and a lot of bending to the bottom shelves. The controlled drugs cage is the one part where you need two people to sign.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters, a bit. If I get it right, somebody's nan gets her heart tablets on time. What wears me out is that they cut us from 40 hours to 35 in the summer after we lost a contract, and my partner Luis is a roofer, so in winter he's half the work. I've got maybe two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then we can stop talking about it and talk about hours. That's what I'd say at work. I don't really go online about stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my problem. My problem is the 35 hours and my partner being off roofing in January. If nothing changes, nothing gets better either, and the company is still looking for another contract to replace the one we lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my pick accuracy up, because they keep the accurate ones when they cut. I'd cut the phone contract down and stop the gym, that's £45 a month. I'd ask my mum if we can have Sunday dinners there through the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but the same worried as now. It's not a new feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the company doesn't find a new contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's another round of cuts, maybe redundancies. There's one other big warehouse near us, and it's agency only. I'd go agency if I had to, but you never know your hours there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum says get a job at the hospital, cleaning or the stores. She's not wrong, but I don't like change, I've been at the warehouse eight years. I'd only go if they pushed me.

I'd say it at work only; I don't really **go online** about things.
think: AI was never my problem; the **35 hours** and my partner's winter gap are.
The company still hasn't **replaced the contract** it lost.
do: Keep **pick accuracy** high, because the accurate ones are kept when cuts come.
Cut the **phone contract** and gym, saving about £45 a month.
Ask her mum for **Sunday dinners** through the winter.
feel: **Worried**, but the same worry she already carries, not a new one.

fieldNote: Her hours were **already cut** after a lost contract, so AI Plateau leaves her anxious.

Her mum pushes the **hospital**; she'd only go if pushed.

steps.text: Keep pick accuracy high to stay off any cut list
Cut the phone contract and gym, about £45 a month
Have Sunday dinners at her mum's through the winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll be the office first, ordering and customer calls, not us. That's what everyone would say at break. I'd say let's see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the ordering lady, Pam, sets our pick waves, and that's the bit software takes. Then they'll start looking at those picking robots for small items, because tablets are small and all the same shape. Tablets are small and all the same shape, so a pharmacy warehouse is the easiest one to automate. All boxes, no weird stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see, first. I'd keep going in and keep my accuracy up. If they announced robots I'd ask about the controlled drugs cage, because they'll always want a person to sign for that. And I'd keep the spending cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like my stomach knows before my head does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wait and see. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A letter. If they put a letter in our lockers, I'd look. Until then I'd just do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn anything new, like the scanning software or the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me. I don't use AI, I don't trust it with medicines. I'd learn what I have to, nothing more.

say: I'd tell people at break it'll be the **office** first, not us.
I'd say **let's see** before getting worked up.
think: Tablets are small and all one shape, so we're the **easiest warehouse** to automate.
Software takes the **pick waves** first, then robots for small items.
do: Wait and see, keeping **accuracy up** until something is announced.
Ask about the **controlled drugs cage**, where a person must still sign.
Keep the **spending cuts** she already made.
feel: **Anxious**, as if her stomach knows before her head does.
S1.quote: Tablets are small and all the same shape, so a pharmacy warehouse is the easiest one to automate.
fieldNote: Her public line (**office first**) is much calmer than her private view.

steps.text: Wait for a formal letter before looking at other jobs
Ask to move to the controlled drugs cage if robots come
Keep the phone and gym cuts going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say somebody needs to do something, the government or whoever. I'm not political, but you can't just let everyone go at once. I'd sign a petition if it was going round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out by 2031, maybe earlier. The ordering goes in 2028, the robots come after, and I've got nothing else, no licence, no course. Luis would be fine-ish, robots on roofs is a long way off, but he can't carry us both in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask at the hospital stores like my mum says, because that's still hands-on and it's the NHS, sorry, the health service. I'd stop everything extra, no holiday, no going out. I'd probably sign on for whatever help there is when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be checking my locker every day for that letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after AGI here. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps, it's three years. But I'm bad at using time. I'd probably spend two of those three years hoping AGI isn't true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance, we'd sell the car and use Luis's van. Then the flat, maybe, we'd have to move in with my mum. I'd hate it but she'd say yes before I'd finished asking.

say: I'd say **somebody** has to act, because you can't let everyone go at once.
I'd **sign a petition**, though I'm not political.
think: I'd be **out by 2031**, with no licence and no course behind me.
My partner's roofing is safer, but he **can't carry us** both in winter.
do: Ask about **hospital stores** jobs, like her mum suggests.
Stop all extras: **no holiday**, no going out.
Apply for **government help** when it exists.
feel: **Scared**, checking her locker every day for the letter.
S2.quote: I'm bad at using time. I'd probably spend two of those three years hoping AGI isn't true.
fieldNote: She knows the three-year gap helps but admits she'd **waste it** hoping.
Moving in with **her mum** is the real fallback.
Even under pressure she's **not political**; she'd sign, not march.

steps.text: Ask at the hospital stores about picking jobs
Sell the car and share her partner's van
Move in with her mum if hours go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the company to tell us properly what's coming. I'd say that to the manager. They should give us notice and some training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the office stuff, eight for the robots. I'd be 35. That's long enough to slide over to the hospital without a panic, if I actually do it. The job here still goes, I'm sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get an application in at the hospital stores in year two, after I've seen what the warehouse does. I'd try to save £50 a month, which is hard. And I'd keep the accuracy up so if I stay longer I'm the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and anxious mixed, mostly anxious. I hate not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why year two and not year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't like jumping. I'd want to see if the robots are real first, so year one I'd just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Luis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm going to the hospital eventually, and he'd say good. He thinks I should have gone years ago.

say: I'd tell the manager five years is enough to give us **proper notice**.
I'd say they owe us some **training**.
think: I'd be **35** when robots arrive, time to move to the hospital calmly.
The warehouse job **still goes**; I'm sure of that.
do: Apply to **hospital stores** in year two after watching year one.
Try to save **£50 a month**, which is hard.
Keep **accuracy** up so she's last to go if she stays.
feel: Mostly **anxious**, with some unease; she hates **not knowing**.
S3.quote: I don't like jumping. I'd want to see if the robots are real first, so year one I'd just watch.
fieldNote: The extra time lets her plan a **slow, safe** move to the hospital.

steps.text: Watch the warehouse for a year before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, fine, that's ages. I'd say we'll cross that bridge. That's honestly what everyone at work would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AGI, thirteen for the robots, I'd be 40. I'd probably stay too long at the warehouse, that's my worry. But the hours and Luis's winters are still the thing keeping me up, not 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep accuracy up, keep the cuts. Maybe the hospital in five years. I'd want to get the controlled drugs signing so I'm trusted with the stuff people still want a person for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, not much about robots. Same as now, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay too long. What would too long look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably stay too long at the warehouse, that's my worry. Me at 39 still in the same aisle when they bring the robots in. And then trying to start somewhere new. I've watched older pickers do that and it's sad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa on my team, she's 58. They moved her to packing after her back went, and she cried in the canteen. I don't want to be her at 58.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages and we'll cross that bridge.
That's what **everyone at work** would say, honestly.
think: My worry is I'd **stay too long** and be 39 in the same aisle.
The **hours** and my partner's winters still keep me up, not 2039.
do: Keep going with **accuracy** up and spending cuts in place.
Get trained to **sign for controlled drugs**.
Look at the **hospital** in about five years.
feel: **Anxious** about money, hardly at all about robots.
S4.quote: I'd probably stay too long at the warehouse, that's my worry. Me at 39 still in the same aisle when they bring the robots in.
fieldNote: The decade removes **robot fear** but not her existing money worry.

steps.text: Keep picking with high accuracy at the pharmacy warehouse

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I'd waste the time I've got. What would help is someone sitting me down with an actual plan, like, here's the hospital job, here's when you start. I'm not good at making the plan myself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about partners. Everyone asks about my job, but our money is my partner's roofs as well. When he's off in winter it doesn't matter if my job is safe.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks about my job, but our money is my partner's roofs as well. When he's off in winter it doesn't matter if my job is safe.
portrait: **Yara** is 27 and has picked medicines at a pharmacy supplies warehouse for **eight years**.
Her hours were cut to **35** this summer, and her partner's roofing work dries up in winter.
She's pragmatic and **not political**, and she dislikes change and doesn't use AI.
She waits for a **letter in the locker** before moving, with the hospital as her fallback.
She's anxious throughout and **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she knows she would **waste** the time hoping.
whatWouldHelp: Someone handing her a **ready-made plan**, like a hospital job with a start date.
